120.t: Playing as well as ever, practising daily and when he will quit
120.s: He thinks he plays more securely than in the Condon days, practises an hour or more a day, and will quit if he slips.
120.q: fortunately, I've had good health up to this point - my wife too and we've lugged some pretty heavy suitcases around; and travelling, you're lucky if you've got some money in your pocket - you can get your bags taken care of. And, that's what we have to do; I can't lift all those heavy things--

120.t: The nightly drive from New Jersey and never being late
120.s: Playing from ten to four needed no warm-up; he drove forty-two miles up the Hudson nightly and missed only one night, in a snowstorm.
120.q: Well, you see, in those days, I really didn't have to warm up because I played so much. So many hours. I'd just come in --- I'd get there half hour - three-quarters of an hour ahead of time - I'd go down to the basement blow a few toots and I didn't have to do like I have to do now. I have to…

921.t: Daily practice, scales and triple tonguing
921.s: Father practiced daily scales and triple tongue, loved High Society; Harold recalls good clarinetists like Sidney Bean who go unmentioned.
921.q: Scales, always before he started to play anything, he'd run his scales all the time. And he did the same thing with his students and that. They had to do that scale work. In other words, he said you just can't keep up without your scale work. Right. He could run those scales and triple tongue. I…

36.s: Finger facility comes from scale work in all keys; transposing matters more in studio or pit work than in jazz.
36.q: Well, it might probably help maybe in a studio or something like that at the last minute. But in just ordinary jazz, it's not as important as it would be in a pit orchestra.

448.t: Practice advice, tape machine and Bechet's ballet
448.s: Bechet advised stopping when tired, recorded himself, composed, played piano and worked on his ballet.
448.q: Yeah, he used to play a lot and he had a tape machine. By that time, he had one of these brush sound mirrors that had come out around 1948. And they were a very good machine. They were kind of difficult to operate by today's standards.

619.t: Why a player must keep practising
619.s: He says music stays with you only if you play daily; after five years off his fingers, lips and breath control have suffered.
619.ch: Clarinet fingering and the Tio family
619.q: He'd change it just that quick. You know, he was so used to doing it, that he was perfect. He was perfected. Yeah. You see, that's what I tell you about music. If you play music every day, it stays with you. But if you stop for two years, three years, a year, and this way, and pick it up again, and…

277.t: Not touching the clarinet; musicians who stop playing
277.s: He hasn't played in years; they discuss loss of technique and George Mitchell refusing to play.
277.q: Well, I would like... I think sometimes that I would like to play and you pick up the clarinet and your fingers don't move as fast as they used to and your lip gets tired and so you get discouraged and you put it away and you don't touch it again for a long time. And so every time you pick it up it…

189.t: Working for Frank Painia and why he changed bands
189.s: Short stints at the Dew Drop; staying too long creates a rut.
189.q: Well see now the same thing with the Doudrop. I didn't stay there too long. I was there a lot of times. I never would stay there no more than a few months. Then I'd leave and then come back.

5.t: How he practiced while working nights
5.s: He practiced long notes and exercises but could not do much while working nights.
5.q: Like on long notes or scales or something at home or not? Yeah, well, I used to practice long notes and exercises, try to practice exercises. But when I was working at night, I didn't get to do too much practicing because most of the time, after getting off, you'd run around in the up and sleep so…

571.t: Practice habits and the low versus high register
571.s: He practises in the low register, argues for its beauty, and discusses weaving high and low with Acker Bilk and Bill Shea.
571.q: I use the, I use the, I use the low register, and, I use the low register, and, I use the low register, to get my lips set that sort of time. No special, No special thing, no way. But, most of my practices, if I'm gonna practice, I'll play something, a little hammer, or something like that, or, a…

726.t: Practicing on a pad to build the wrists
726.s: Cie has no practice pad and they talk about making one from rubber. Williams advises constant practice on a pad with two sticks, whistling the tune, to strengthen the wrists, and talks about drum heads.
726.q: I thought he... I didn't know he... He rolls nice. Oh, you gotta do this practice. That's all that's in the line of drumming this person. Constant practice is like a man doing that guitar. See them guys with them guitars, they got the practice, they chords. And, of course, while they're playing the…

58.t: Learning practical tricks from retired players
58.s: Punch and Zango talk about professors versus practical tips, and Punch says retired players share most.
58.q: All right. Ain't like them professors, you know. Some of them questions I can answer, but take a man like Joe Hodden and he can answer more than anything he asks.

615.s: He quotes a Van Eps saying about practice and describes his routine.
615.q: Oh, right. I was paraphrasing someone else. I think it dates back to one of the great classical musicians or something. I heard it from George Van Eps, via George Van Eps. Yeah, if I don’t practice for one day I notice it; if I don’t practice for two days, the conductor notices it; and if I don’t…

1028.t: Staying motivated: the Mark Masters CD and being ready for a call
1028.s: Baron fakes it till he makes it, recalls preparing for a CD with Mark Masters, and sets his own practice goals in case a gig comes.
1028.q: Well it varies. Sometimes I just have to do the “act as if” or “fake it ‘til you make it” kind of idea. Because like when I have something, you know, to look forward to, like I did a

673.t: Practice, never mastering the instrument, improvisation
673.s: Both stress daily practice, that you never master the horn, and that soloing is composing on your feet.
673.q: You’ve got to understand that you never, not only do you never learn it, but you’ve never got it down perfect either. Ever. Every time you pick the thing up it’s a challenge.

598.t: Staying active, practicing and keeping time
598.s: He plays jazz parties and clubs from Palm Springs, practices daily, and says rhythm sections hate players without time.
598.q: Well that is nice. I like when people come up to me and say I hear you on certain records and this and that, and I look forward to that. And of course some people say, “Oh you moved to Palm Springs, did you retire?” And I say well, “No I don’t think they’ll let me retire.” As long as they keep…

926.t: Learning solos and the demands of practice
926.s: Practice as a lonely art, 'Flying Home', 'Cool Blues' solos people expected.
926.q: Well endurance, you have to learn how to practice also. Because without the drudgery of practice, practice is not as pretty as what’s seen as a performer, or as you see a performer perform. Practice is a lonely art. It’s very demeaning sometimes when you have to practice something over and over and…

1017.t: Duet and Dialogue, staying in the moment, practicing on the bandstand
1017.s: Asked how life changed his music since 1976, he says he stays in the moment, practices heads and piano, and the bandstand is his real practice.
1017.ch: Playing and listening in the moment
1017.q: Well I’m sure it has. I don’t think about things like that if I’m understanding your question clearly. I really don’t think about things like that. It’s important for me to stay in the moment and so I won’t spend time — yeah, I don’t know if I’m answering your question correctly. I don’t consider…

599.t: Lambert, Hendricks & Ross and muscle memory
599.s: How Jon Hendricks sings so fast: tedious repetition; Gates on watching himself on video and Freddie Freeloader.
599.q: It’s amazing what he wrote, and that he sings a John Coltrane solo. I mean who could sing a John Coltrane solo? Jon Hendricks.

898.t: Goals and advice for students: practice in small steps
898.s: He sets goals for touring, film scoring and band pay, and advises students on simple practice goals, citing Wynton Marsalis's metronome practice.
898.q: Sure. I have a goal where I want to be much more, believe it or not, on tour with me and my own groups. I have goals where I’d like to write for a major motion picture or write for some type of film, to continue this. Goals to be a much better saxophonist. So you have goals to have earnings for…

542.t: What he practices now: hard tunes slowly, and rests
542.s: Johnstone practices difficult changes slowly, as with Giant Steps as a ballad; the Vido Musso story about trouble with the rests.
542.q: I practice things that are hard. I practice tunes that have different chord changes, things that don’t lay correctly. And they don’t lay naturally under my hands. And so I’ll work them slowly. Back when I was learning “Giant Steps” I practiced it as a ballad. And gradually got where the most…

793.s: Mayhew has done karate for over thirty years and practices saxophone early in the day; her practice has changed little in decades. Caring for her late parents cut into her karate.
793.q: I do. I’ve been doing karate a long time. It’s been life changing actually. I’ve been doing it since I first moved to New York so that’s over thirty years.

346.t: Practising, memory work and Jackie McLean's book
346.s: Discussing playing Nonaah, he describes working on memorization and recommends Jackie McLean's exercise book.
346.ch: Performing and the idea of free jazz
346.q: Yeah, that’s a good book man, he takes you to all those choruses and so on and then at the end you have the grand exercises and so on and so on and so forth you know. I mean Jackie Mac is a mean individual. You know. I mean [scats] you know, the thing on

415.t: Losing motivation to practice, sorting the storage room
415.s: Being a musician is a life, not a job; he and Dick Hyman lost the will to practice, and he is sifting sheet music for new sets. Talking with other musicians is depressing.
415.q: Yeah. And I think, I’ve had this conversation with friends of mine. I think sometimes it’s hard for a lot of non-musicians to really understand our plight because it’s not a job. You know if you’re a musician it’s you, it’s your life. And so your income is taken away and part of your being is taken…

596.t: Practicing and staying sharp: Wild Bill Davison, Jane Jarvis, Randy Weston
596.s: Prompted by his Jamey Aebersold practice, Powell says nothing comes easily and compares how Wild Bill Davison, Jane Jarvis and Randy Weston keep up their playing.
596.q: Man, I was in Germany with Wild Bill Davison, the old cornet player, and man he had his little audiotape that he — and by this time he was about 387 years old, I mean this guy was old, but he had this little walkman and he put his tape on, put his cup mute in and got ready for the gig. Well I think…

547.t: Study, scoring and practice as a musician without gigs
547.s: He copies out scores by Don Sebesky and Thad Jones note by note and argues that one should keep practicing so as to be ready when gigs return.
547.q: I think it depends on the person and how we handled it. Like for me, even if I was to stop playing in public it doesn’t mean that I stop playing you know. I’m still going to be like well for the past three months I’ve been at home mostly. Like I said I practice, I’ve been studying. Every morning I…

992.t: Gaps in her training and honest practice
992.s: She still feels her time and basics are shaky and works on finding what is not working.
992.q: Just I swear it’s like simple stuff you know. I still feel that sometimes my time is wiggly woggly and just like sometimes my ideas they don’t — you know they are simple things that probably for any beginner musician will be the first step that you do it. And I skipped some of the steps because…

356.t: How he improvises and keeps in shape
356.s: Improvising on automatic pilot, practice, and keeping the trumpet lip in shape.
356.q: Well I’m trying to play those chords, and play interesting notes in the chords, and rhythm, and I have be really, a lot of it has to be on automatic pilot, because I can’t think of it. That’s why I have to practice so much, so that I get my body just kind of playing. And then I can almost listen to…

425.t: Advice on practicing and music as compulsion
425.s: Practice in short sessions, keep analyzing music all day; musicians are diseased with a compulsion for music.
425.ch: Life on the road and advice
425.q: Well let’s see. From the point of view of practicing as a trumpet player, we’re all concerned with endurance. Because it hurts to play the instrument. What I did was when it started to hurt I put the horn down. So instead of practicing an hour and a half at a clip, I may do thirty minutes three…

611.s: Age does not matter, education and practice do, and he practices more than ever now.
611.q: And then practice makes perfect is the old saying you know? You practice, you know? You can’t just stay in — age hasn’t really much to do with it. I mean that’s, I’ve had that argument so much in Europe, you know. A lot of people think when you get old you can’t play this or you can’t play that.…

85.s: He now practices only before performances, often playing along with a record.
85.q: If I don’t practice . . . oh, boy. Oh, if I don’t practice for . . . gee, sorry I don’t remember this correctly, but it’s like if I don’t practice for some length of time, I know it, and if I don’t practice for . . . oh, I don’t know it. I can’t remember it, but it’s first I know it, then you know…

368.t: Hand in Hand with Hannon and his practice routine
368.s: His Hannon exercise book and his daily routine.
368.ch: Later life, Terry Gibbs and Artie Shaw
368.q: Well, yeah, that was a brainstorm of mine and it worked out pretty good, it turned out to be a good clarinet exercise book. And what I did was transcribed Hannon’s exercise, about twelve of them, in every key for the clarinet. Turns out to be a good study for clarinetists. I get letters from time…

143.s: He did not practice much; he changed keys to stay fresh.
143.q: I was working a lot then. I didn’t have no practice routine. When I started playing a lot, I never practiced, because I’d just go to work. If I got tired of playing a song, I just played it another key or something like that. Keep myself fresh. It made me think about what I’m doing.

369.t: Warm-up exercises: Czerny, Hanon and the weak fingers
369.s: She warms up with Czerny, Hanon and Brahms exercises, and discusses strengthening the fourth and fifth fingers.
369.q: It is, and you just have to practice it until you get tired and hold the others down. But these two, you have to use them a lot.

371.t: Maintaining technique: scales and daily practice
371.s: He still practices at least two hours a day, stressing scales and arpeggios.
371.ch: Pontiac childhood, family and piano training
371.q: Maintaining technique is a daily routine. You can never get away from practicing the basics, I mean scales in all the keys, exercises, special exercises of various difficulties, running through thirds, and the crossing over of the thumb— scales! You’d be surprised that scales and arpeggios are…

651.s: He has little practice time, thinks music constantly, finds the sax easier since about 50, and his wife senses he is practicing.
651.q: I don’t. That’s simple. I just don’t have time to practice. Or I don’t make time to practice. But I’m thinking music all the time. I tell people... I’m 74. I tell them, “I started the sax at age 12, and at about age 50, the saxophone gave in. It said, ‘Jamey is not going to stop. So why don’t we…

508.t: Practicing classical repertoire because it will not let him escape
508.s: Classical music like the Creston sonata forces him to face his inadequacies, unlike jazz, which lets you change songs to suit you.
508.q: I’m always practicing specific repertoire pieces. I’m always practicing them. Even when I’m not…. Like I’m playing the Creston Sonata. I’ve never played the Creston, ever. But I’ve been practicing it for years. I always play these pieces, because they are the things…. I mean, jazz is very personal.…

114.t: Practicing on the road and in his head
114.s: He practices flute in the morning and in his head in hotels and on buses, writing out ideas later.
114.ch: Practice, the road and Dizzy's death
114.q: Well, it depends, like, if I'm getting up early in the morning, usually, I get up and I usually have some tea or something and then I'll take my flute and try to play a couple notes before I go because if I don't, I get a little depressed because, you know, you're playing something out there, but…

17.t: Practice setup, photos and wrapping up the session
17.ch: Life in Columbus and recent activity
17.q: Yes, I know. But that's one reason why I like this apartment I have, as you see it's on the ground floor, it doesn't bother with anybody and I've got my little tapes and my little record players, my little earphones in there and I can just get in there and get my chops up good and wail until I fall…

67.t: Daily listening and practice; Harold Baker's recording
67.s: He listens to Clifford Brown, Miles and Harold Baker, writes down ideas daily, practices, does not drink, and rests.
67.q: He always give me credit for that. Well, Benny Carter turned out to be an exceptional trumpet player. And I listen to his records, all the time; His trumpet playing. And I like Clifford Brown, as I say, he's one of my favorites and I like -- I listen to Miles Davis, a lot. The things that I…

68.s: Tate says he practised all day when young, less with Basie, and now nearly as much as ever.
68.ch: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
68.q: : Well, not as much as I used to. I -- well, actually, well, I would say, after I joined in Basie -- you know, we played every night. So I didn't have a chance, you know. But I practice more now than I did when I was with Basie's band, because I have days off and I have time in my home and I have…

146.t: Never practised scales or used instruction books
146.s: Smith never bought instruction books or practised scales, only worked out melodies and ideas.
146.ch: Opening and early years in Dallas

70.t: How to practice: long soft notes, scales, instrument before solos
70.s: Jackson recommends whole notes played softly on the trombone, scales slowly, and mastering the instrument before soloing.
70.ch: After the road: New York, the profession and advice
70.q: I -- first thing, if he's a piano player, he should find correct fingerings. You have five finger exercises, which is a great help as far as the piano is concerned.

18.s: Neither he nor Hawkins practiced, only playing on the job for half an hour.
18.ch: Cincinnati, Buffalo, Russell and Fletcher Henderson
18.q: Get on the job and play about a half hour - because we knew the tunes of some of the music we had to read. We had the music all the time.

86.t: Trumpet endurance, laying off, and spontaneous jazz
86.s: Edison says he dislikes practising, and compares jazz spontaneity to studio work.
86.q: Just has to keep his muscles right there, see. But a trumpet player, man, he can lay off his horn for days and come back, you know. Only thing he looses is he's got to get his fingers together. But when you lay off of a trumpet, you have one little spot that you can play there.
